extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies; journalism professionals and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative standards for journalistic ethics, newsworthiness, and newsroom routines—how journalists should act, how to assess ethical dilemmas, and the routine criteria that determine what becomes news. Geared toward understanding newsroom decision-making and content selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and public dialogue (SPJ code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should be accountable to the public for their reports and the public should be encouraged to voice its grievances against the media. Open dialogue with our readers, viewers, and listeners should be fostered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to this code is intended to preserve and strengthen mutual trust and respect between journalists and the public. Societies and news organizations should encourage individual journalists to adhere to these tenets and should frame codes of ethics in concert with employees as guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ guiding principles
rubrics_metrics.description: "Seek truth and report is as fully as possible; act independently; and minimize harm."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are basic guiding principles recommended for assessing ethical decisions in journalism; they serve as core values to balance when making publication choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten-question ethical assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether a situation may be unethical, journalists should ask: (1) What do I know? What do I need to know? (2) What is my journalistic purpose? (3) What are my ethical concerns? (4) What organizational policies and professional guidelines should I consider? (5) How can I include other people, with different perspectives and diverse ideas, in the decision-making process? (6) Who are the stakeholders—those affected by my decision? What are their motivations? Which are legitimate? (7) What if the roles were reversed? How would I feel if I were in the shoes of one of the stakeholders? (8) What are the possible consequences of my actions? Short-term? Long-term? (9) What are my alternatives to maximize my truth-telling responsibility and minimize harm? (10) Can I clearly and fully justify my thinking and my decision? To my colleagues? To the stakeholders? To the public?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a structured deliberation tool when facing ethical dilemmas; it codifies reflective questions to balance truth-telling, independence, and harm-minimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should avoid conflicts such as holding stock in local companies, and while some consider receiving tickets and meals acceptable, other gifts and free trips generally are not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational codes (e.g., Minneapolis Star, Los Angeles Times, Washington Post) explicitly warn about financial or personal ties to sources; controversy over 'junket journalism' (industry-paid trips) illustrates reputational and ethical risk—news organizations should have clear policies and consider reimbursing or refusing inappropriate freebies.

rubrics_metrics.name: No misrepresentation / full attribution (including VNRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrepresentation centers on whether a story could have been obtained another way; use of video news releases (VNRs) or republishing material produced by outside PR firms without clear attribution is an abdication of a news organization's ethical responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a news operation uses a VNR in its entirety and without attribution, the viewer incorrectly believes the news organization produced the story; hiding the true producer of a message undermines credibility. Avoid staging, rigging tests (Dateline NBC example), or any deception that misleads viewers about how evidence was obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photography and digital-image manipulation ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Digitalization of photographs makes it possible to manipulate images in ways previously undetectable; many photo editors object to manipulation beyond traditional dodging and burning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish limits on acceptable image editing; be transparent about any alterations and avoid deceptive manipulation that changes the substantive meaning of an image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source confidentiality and 'outing' considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical problems arise regarding revealing sources' private information (e.g., 'outing' sexual orientation); many journalists oppose outing as a violation of privacy, though some argue differential treatment of public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the public interest and privacy harms; confidentiality is highly valued (only a small percentage would justify divulging confidential sources), and decisions about revealing private details require justification within ethical principles and organizational policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming victims, juveniles, and privacy-sensitive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey-identified ethical dilemmas include naming rape victims, naming juveniles in crime stories, and reporting names/addresses of crime victims—areas of special concern for potential harm and privacy invasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider potential additional suffering to victims/families, privacy laws, and community standards; err on the side of minimizing harm unless a compelling public interest justifies identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of undercover methods, payments, and document use
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists differ on practices such as claiming to be someone else to get a story, paying people for confidential information, using personal documents without permission, badgering unwilling informants, or going undercover; acceptance varies by age, organizational size, and role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These intrusive methods carry ethical risks and require strong editorial oversight and justification; organizational norms and professional socialization strongly influence acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: News judgment as application of news values
rubrics_metrics.description: News judgment is the ability to evaluate stories based on agreed-on news values, which provide yardsticks of newsworthiness and predict what an audience will find appealing and important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News judgment institutionalizes audience expectations into routinized craft norms; use it to make consistent gatekeeping decisions when direct audience feedback is unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: Prominence / Importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of a story is measured in its impact: how many lives it affects. Fatalities are more important than property damage. Actions of the powerful are newsworthy because what the powerful do affects the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize stories with larger societal impact and those involving powerful actors whose actions affect many people.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: People are interested in items that don't directly affect their lives—celebrities, political gossip, and human dramas; stories with a human element elicit this kind of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate issues through affected people to increase audience engagement, especially in television which often uses human-angle storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: Conflict / Controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict signals important issues and is inherently more interesting than harmony; controversy alerts audiences to issues of disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to stories that reveal or involve conflict, as conflict often heightens newsworthiness and audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: The unusual
rubrics_metrics.description: The unusual interests audiences because it deviates from everyday expectations; exceptional events stand out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include novel or surprising elements that deviate from routine occurrences to attract and hold audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: News is timely—events happening now are prioritized because audiences want to know what's happening immediately and timely events may require action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize current events; timeliness increases perceived urgency and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that happen near the audience are considered more newsworthy; local events usually have more effect than distant ones. Local media seek local angles in national stories to better interest the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek local relevance or angles to national/international stories to increase audience interest and perceived impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid story structure (routine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverted pyramid routine places facts in order of decreasing importance so readers can stop after a few paragraphs knowing they've read the most important information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves both audience and organizational needs: readers get top facts early; editors can trim from the bottom to meet space constraints without rewriting the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-routines constraints triangle (audience/organization/suppliers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media routines stem from constraints related to three stages: consumers (audience), the organization (capability to process), and suppliers (sources). Routines help answer: (1) What is acceptable to the consumer? (2) What is the organization capable of processing? (3) What product is available from suppliers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize routines as balancing these three constraints; individual routines may serve audience, organization, supplier needs in varying proportions (e.g., inverted pyramid serves audience and organization). Use this model to evaluate why certain routines exist and how they shape content selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television news routinization / 'news factory' norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Television news often resembles a 'news factory' with high turnover, specialized roles, heavy coordination of complex technologies, reliance on consultants prescribing formulaic guidelines (number and length of stories), and an emphasis on technically uniform, visually sophisticated, fast-paced, people-oriented stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These organizational routines prioritize efficiency and predictability, often valuing speed and packaging over depth ('quick and dirty' stories). Recognize these norms when evaluating TV news content quality and constraints on reporters' autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional role orientation (disseminator vs interpreter) effect on content
rubrics_metrics.description: How journalists define their job (disseminator/neutral vs interpreter/participant) affects the content they produce; students who saw themselves as neutrals wrote less fair/comprehensive stories, while those midway between neutral and participant produced the most objective and accurate stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider self-conception of role when evaluating possible bias and comprehensiveness; professional roles and ethics often have greater influence on content than personal attitudes alone.
